extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and educated readers/writers (Elizabethan-era dramatists and poets)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical standards for composing and staging poetry and plays in English—covering unity of action, use of time/place, genre boundaries (tragedy vs comedy), diction, similitude, imitation of the ancients, and versification choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action / begin at the principal point (not ab ovo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy ought not to begin 'ab ovo' but must come to the principal point of that one action which it will represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin the represented action at its crucial incident rather than narrating the whole history from the origin. Example: in the Polydorus story Euripides begins at the finding of the body rather than at the child's delivery—this economizes place and time and makes the action intelligible on stage. Use reported speech (Nuntius) for events that precede the represented action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of tragedy from strict historical sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is tied to the laws of poesy, not of history; it is not bound to follow the chronological story but may feign new matter or frame history to tragic convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet-playwright may compress, alter, or invent events when doing so serves the tragic effect and unity of the action. Do not mistake fidelity to historical chronology for fidelity to poetic/tragic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible representation of place and time on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically represent many places and many times on a single stage without conventions or preface; stage presentation must be believable within theatrical convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid far-fetched stage shifts that force the audience to supply implausible leaps (e.g., three ladies gathered in a garden, then immediate news of a shipwreck and a monster). If many places or times are involved use devices like a Nuntius or reported narration; give the audience the necessary information or compress the action to a manageable setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing inappropriate elements of spectacle and artless representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on crude stage contrivances (hideous monsters with smoke, armies represented by a few swords and bucklers) that make the representation absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle that contradicts sense or exceeds the stage's capacity for believable signification damages poetic effect. The audience should not be compelled to constantly supply impossible settings in imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper distinction between tragedy and comedy (avoid mongrel tragi-comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays that mingle kings and clowns, not because the matter requires it, but by thrusting clowns into majestic matters, produce neither right tragedy nor right comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the tragic action in a maintained tone of admiration and commiseration; keep comedy full of delight and proper to its social level. If mixing is used, it should be done sparingly and with craft so that neither admiration nor delight is lost (ancients did this rarely and delicately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic ends: delight plus teaching, not mere laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of the comical part is not mere laughter; comedy should mix delightful teaching with its mirth and not make laughter the sole aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter often arises from disproportion and scorn, whereas delight arises from what is agreeable or beneficial. Comedy should aim to instruct or delight, not simply to provoke scornful laughter. Avoid making fun of things that are execrable or pitiable (e.g., wretched beggars, strangers mocked for language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical suitability of comic targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not stir laughter at sinful or miserable things which are rather to be execrated or pitied than ridiculed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ridicule of affectations, pride, or folly (e.g., a busy loving courtier, a self-wise schoolmaster) rather than mockery of genuine suffering or violations of hospitality. The comic should align with moral teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of diction; avoid affected eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'honey-flowing matron eloquence' and painted affectation—far-fetched words, unnatural coinages, and over-flowery figures that make writers seem monsters or strangers to common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, natural expression that persuades rather than rhetorical ornament for its own sake. Imitate the effect of Cicero and Demosthenes by absorbing their art, but do not slavishly transplant their phrases; do not 'show art' but 'hide art.' Avoid forcing elaborate rhetorical figures where the tone does not call for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of rhetorical figures (repetition, cadences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical devices (e.g., repetition, cadences) are valuable but must fit the emotion and context; used wrongly they become sophistry or mere ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition (as Cicero does in choler) where emotional intensity warrants it; avoid using such devices habitually in contexts where they seem curious rather than persuasive—this creates the appearance of fineness without persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious use of similitudes and similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Similitudes are useful only to explain to a willing hearer; when their purpose is fulfilled further similitudes become tedious and distract from the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ comparisons sparingly and only when they clarify; do not 'rifle up' multitudes of similes from herbalists or bestiaries to parade conceits—overuse oversways memory from the purpose rather than informing judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate the ancients by assimilation, not slavish copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators of classical authors should not keep lists of their figures and phrases to be transplanted whole, but should by attentive translation devour them and make them wholly theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the best of ancient models but adapt them to natural speech and the needs of English poetry. Avoid casting 'sugar and spice' upon every line; persuasion and truthful expression are higher aims than feigned fineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose versification suited to language and musical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two sorts of versifying: the ancient (quantity) and the modern (number/rhyme). The English is well-suited to both due to its accentual properties and capacity for masculine/feminine/sdrucciola endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the metric system that best achieves musicality and expresses passions properly. Recognize the relative strengths (quantity for music tied to syllabic weight; rhyme for ear-pleasing effect) and exploit English's strengths (precise accent, caesura, variety of rhyme types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity in the material point of poesy; avoid artificial love-phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Many contemporary love writings use coldly applied fiery speeches and swelling phrases that betray no true passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should convey 'energia'—true force of feeling—so that passion seems felt rather than borrowed from reading. Avoid stock lover clichés used without inward experience; aim for real feeling expressed with force.
